lessons.title: What aquaculture is
lessons.html:
Farming in water

Aquaculture means farming animals and plants that live in water. Instead of catching fish in the sea or a river, we grow them on a farm. It is like farming cattle or chickens, but the animals live in water.

What is farmed

  • Fish: such as trout, tilapia and catfish.
  • Shellfish: such as abalone, mussels and oysters.
  • Plants: such as seaweed.

Where it happens

  • Freshwater: dams, ponds, tanks and rivers. Fresh water has no salt.
  • Marine (sea water): tanks on the coast, or ropes and rafts in a bay.

Why aquaculture is important

  • The sea has fewer wild fish than before. Many fish stocks are overfished.
  • People need protein. Fish is healthy food.
  • Aquaculture creates jobs, also in rural areas.
  • Fish and shellfish can be sold in South Africa and to other countries.

Aquaculture and other farming

Some farmers keep fish in a farm dam and also grow vegetables. The water from the fish tanks has fish waste in it. This waste is good fertiliser for plants. Growing fish and plants together is called aquaponics.

Aquaculture is still a small industry in South Africa, but it is growing. You are joining an industry with a future.

lessons.title: The aquaculture industry in South Africa
lessons.html:
Where farms are

AreaWhat is farmed
Western Cape coast (Hermanus, Saldanha Bay)Abalone, mussels, oysters
Southern Cape (Knysna)Oysters
Mountain areas of the Western Cape and MpumalangaTrout in cold, clean water
Warmer areas such as Limpopo, KwaZulu-Natal and North WestTilapia and catfish
Many placesOrnamental fish such as koi

People in the industry

  • Farm workers: feed the animals, clean tanks, check water, harvest.
  • Farm managers and farmers: plan the work and run the business.
  • Hatchery workers: breed animals and grow the babies.
  • Processing workers: clean, pack and freeze the product.
  • Suppliers: sell feed, equipment and baby fish.
  • Government officials: give permits and check farms.

Rules for aquaculture farms

Aquaculture farms need permits from government. Some fish that are farmed, like trout, are not from South Africa. They can harm rivers if they escape. So there are rules about which fish may be farmed and where. Sea farms must also follow the Marine Living Resources Act 18 of 1998. Water use is controlled by the National Water Act 36 of 1998. Your farm manager handles the permits, but you must help by following the rules on the farm.

lessons.title: Working safely and well on a fish farm
lessons.html:
Your job on the farm

A good aquaculture worker:

  • Feeds the animals on time with the right amount of feed.
  • Watches the animals every day and reports problems.
  • Checks the water and writes down the results.
  • Keeps tanks, nets and equipment clean.
  • Stops fish from escaping.
  • Follows the hygiene rules so diseases do not spread.

Dangers on a fish farm

  • Drowning: ponds, dams and the sea are deep. Never work alone near deep water. Wear a life jacket on boats, rafts and cages.
  • Slipping: wet floors and pond banks are slippery. Wear boots with a good grip.
  • Electricity: pumps and aerators use electricity near water. Never touch electrical equipment with wet hands. Report damaged cables.
  • Lifting: feed bags and full nets are heavy. Bend your knees and ask for help.
  • Chemicals: some treatments and disinfectants are dangerous. Wear gloves and read the label.
  • Sun and cold: wear a hat and sunscreen in summer, and warm clothes in winter.

Your rights

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 says your employer must keep the workplace safe and train you. You must follow safety rules and report dangers.

Key points

  • Aquaculture is farming animals and plants that live in water.
  • South Africa farms abalone, mussels, oysters, trout, tilapia, catfish and koi.
  • Farms need permits, and fish must not escape.
  • Never work alone near deep water and wear a life jacket on boats.
  • Keep electricity away from water and report damaged cables.
